title: The Cell: A Unit of Life
tagline: Cell theory, the sizes and shapes of cells, every major organelle, and the plant-versus-animal difference.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every statement below is standard cell biology. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Every living thing is built from cells, and this chapter explains why the cell is called the unit of life. It opens with the three parts of cell theory and the scientists associated with them, then shows how wildly cells differ in size and shape while sharing the same basic plan. The bulk of the chapter is a guided tour of the organelles — what each one looks like and, more importantly, what it actually does. It closes with the two comparisons that examiners ask about most: prokaryote against eukaryote, and plant cell against animal cell.

learningOutcomes: State cell theory and name the contribution of Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow to it.
Describe the size and shape range of cells and relate an unusual cell shape to its function.
Identify each organelle in a labelled diagram and state its function in one sentence.
Distinguish prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells and plant cells from animal cells in a table.

learn.title: Cell theory and the form of cells

blocks.text: Cell theory was built in three steps. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden, studying plant tissues, reported that all plants are made of cells. In 1839 Theodor Schwann extended the claim to animals and added that the cell is the basic structural unit of life. Their statement was still incomplete, because it could not explain how a new cell arises. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow supplied the missing piece with the Latin phrase omnis cellula e cellula — every cell comes from a pre-existing cell — after observing cell division in diseased tissue. Modern cell theory adds two further points: cells contain hereditary material that is passed on, and all cells use the same basic chemical reactions. A cell is typically between 1 and 100 micrometres across, so a centimetre holds about ten thousand of them in a row.

items.meaning: The statement that all living organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells arise only from existing cells.
One millionth of a metre, written micrometre or micrometre symbol; the unit in which cell size is normally quoted.
A cell with no true membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane organelles — bacteria and blue-green algae.
A cell with a true nucleus bounded by a nuclear envelope and with membrane-bound organelles.
A specialised structure inside a cell that carries out a particular function, analogous to an organ in a body.

items: Schleiden (1838) — all plant tissue is cellular; Schwann (1839) — all animals are cellular and the cell is the unit of life.
Virchow (1855) — every cell arises from a pre-existing cell, which completed the theory.
Cells range from about 0.25 micrometres (some bacteria) to the hen's egg yolk at about 4 centimetres.
The nerve cell is the longest cell in the body, stretching from the spinal cord to the toes, because it must carry impulses over that distance.
Shape follows function: a nerve cell is thread-like for transmission, a red blood cell is a biconcave disc for carrying oxygen, and a root hair cell is a long tube for absorption.
A cell is bounded by a membrane called the plasmalemma, and in plants by an additional rigid cell wall outside it.

items.text: Shape for function: the root hair cell of a moss has a long extension that increases surface area for absorbing water from the soil.
items.note: An elongated shape is only useful because it raises the surface-area-to-volume ratio.

items.text: Shape for function: the human sperm cell has a whip-like tail (flagellum) that pushes it along, while its mid-piece is packed with mitochondria for the energy this needs.
items.note: Two structures in one cell, each matched to a different task.

learn.title: The organelles and what each one does

blocks.text: A eukaryotic cell is a compartmentalised factory, and each compartment is an organelle. The nucleus holds the cell's DNA as chromatin and controls all activity by switching genes on and off; it is enclosed in a double nuclear envelope pierced by pores that let RNA escape. Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration, where energy is released and trapped as ATP; they have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and they carry their own DNA. The endoplasmic reticulum is a folded membrane network continuous with the nuclear envelope: rough ER studded with ribosomes makes proteins, while smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages those proteins into vesicles for delivery. Ribosomes, which are not membrane-bound, are the actual sites of protein synthesis. Lysosomes are Golgi vesicles packed with hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles and trapped bacteria.

blocks.caption: Organelles, their structure and their function
rows: Support, protection, prevents bursting on over-hydration
Controls what enters and leaves the cell
Double envelope with pores; contains chromatin
Controls cell activities; stores hereditary material
Double membrane, inner folded into cristae
Aerobic respiration; releases energy as ATP
Rough ER makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids
Digests worn-out parts and captured microbes
Fluid-filled sac; large and permanent in plants

items: Mitochondria are called the power houses because aerobic respiration there yields far more ATP than glycolysis alone.
Rough ER looks rough because ribosomes are attached to its outer surface.
Lysosomes are sometimes called suicide bags: if they burst, their enzymes digest the cell itself.
Ribosomes free in the cytoplasm make proteins for the cell's own use; bound ribosomes make proteins for export.
The nuclear envelope is a double membrane, so the nucleus has two membranes while the mitochondrion also has two.
Plant cells contain plastids — chloroplasts for photosynthesis, chromoplasts for colour, leucoplasts for storage.

items.text: A pancreatic cell that secretes digestive enzyme is crowded with rough ER and Golgi, because the protein must be synthesised, modified and packaged for export.
items.note: Cells that secrete a lot show the protein-making pathway in exaggerated form.

items.text: A white blood cell that has engulfed a bacterium surrounds it in a vesicle that fuses with a lysosome, and the enzymes destroy the invader.
items.note: This is why lysosome numbers rise in a cell under attack.

blocks.text: The deepest split in cell biology is between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotes — bacteria, blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) and mycoplasma — have no nucleus: their circular DNA sits free in a region called the nucleoid, with no enclosing membrane. They also lack every membrane-bound organelle, so there are no mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi apparatus; their ribosomes are smaller and their plasma membrane is the only membrane they possess. Eukaryotic cells, by contrast, package their DNA inside a true nucleus and divide their work among membrane-bound compartments, which lets each organelle hold its own chemical conditions. Eukaryotic cells arose, according to the endosymbiotic theory, when a larger cell engulfed a smaller aerobic bacterium that became the mitochondrion. Prokaryotes are typically 1 to 10 micrometres long and divide by binary fission, a far simpler process than mitosis.

blocks.caption: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells compared
rows: Absent; DNA free in the nucleoid
Present, bounded by a nuclear envelope
Present in plants (cellulose) and fungi, absent in animals

items.meaning: The region of a prokaryotic cell where the circular DNA lies, not surrounded by a membrane.
Division of a prokaryote by simple splitting into two roughly equal daughter cells.
The polymer of sugars and amino acids that gives a bacterial cell wall its strength.
The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell.

items.text: Escherichia coli is a typical prokaryote: about 2 micrometres long, circular DNA in a nucleoid, no nucleus, no mitochondria, and it doubles by binary fission in about twenty minutes under good conditions.
items.note: Quote the size first — prokaryote questions are often opened with a size estimate.

items.text: An amoeba is a eukaryote: it has a nucleus with a membrane, food vacuoles that carry out digestion, and contractile vacuoles that expel excess water.
items.note: Both are single-celled, which is why 'unicellular' is not the difference between them.

blocks.text: Plant and animal cells share the same core machinery — nucleus, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, ribosomes and membrane — but three structures set them apart. A plant cell has a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the membrane, which gives it a fixed rectangular shape and stops it from bursting when it takes in water. It also has a large central permanent vacuole holding cell sap; this pushes the cytoplasm against the wall and creates the turgor pressure that keeps a soft plant upright without any skeleton. Finally, plant cells contain plastids, above all the chloroplasts that carry out photosynthesis. Animal cells have none of these three, so they are bounded by the membrane alone, are round or irregular in shape, and rely on stored glycogen rather than starch. Animal cells usually have small, short-lived vacuoles used for transport rather than storage.

blocks.caption: Plant cell against animal cell
rows: One large permanent central vacuole of cell sap

items: The cell wall is fully permeable — it is the membrane inside it that actually controls entry and exit.
Turgor pressure is what keeps a herbaceous plant firm; a plant wilts when its vacuole loses water and the cell becomes flaccid.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the sites of photosynthesis, so they are found only in the green, light-exposed parts of a plant.
Animal cells cannot make cellulose, so their outline is set by the membrane and they can change shape.
A plant cell may be said to have two membrane systems — the plasma membrane and the tonoplast around the vacuole — while an animal cell has one.
Both cell types carry out respiration in mitochondria; only the plant cell can also trap light energy.

items.text: A leaf cell in bright light is packed with chloroplasts lining the cytoplasm so that each one receives light, while the same plant's root cell has no chloroplasts because it never sees light.
items.note: Use this to show that organelles are distributed according to need, not by rule.

items.text: Dropping a plant cell into a concentrated salt solution draws water out of its vacuole, so the membrane shrinks from the wall — the cell is plasmolysed. An animal cell in the same solution simply shrivels, because there is no wall to separate from.
items.note: The same osmotic stress, two different visible outcomes.

figures.caption: Figure: A generalised plant cell
figures.description: A rectangular cell drawn with a thick outer cell wall and a thin membrane just inside it. The nucleus sits to one side, pushed there by a large central vacuole bounded by a tonoplast. Chloroplasts and mitochondria are scattered in the thin band of cytoplasm between the vacuole and the wall, and rough ER is drawn next to the nuclear envelope.

figures.caption: Figure: A generalised animal cell and its organelles
figures.description: An irregular rounded outline bounded only by the cell membrane. Centrally placed nucleus with pores, a Golgi apparatus drawn as a stack of curved sacs budding off vesicles, mitochondria with cristae shown as inner folds, lysosomes as small dark vesicles, and ribosomes as dots both free in the cytoplasm and attached to rough ER.

figures.caption: Figure: Prokaryotic cell against eukaryotic cell
figures.description: On the left a rod-shaped bacterium with a cell wall, a plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the nucleoid, scattered 70S ribosomes and a capsule. On the right an animal cell with a membrane-bound nucleus, linear chromosomes, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes. The absence of any internal membrane on the left is the point of the comparison.

keyPoints: Cell theory: Schleiden (1838) plants, Schwann (1839) animals and the cell as unit of life, Virchow (1855) every cell from a pre-existing cell.
Cell size is quoted in micrometres; the hen's egg yolk is the largest cell and the nerve cell the longest.
Shape follows function — nerve cells are thread-like, red blood cells are biconcave discs, root hairs are long tubes.
The nucleus is bounded by a double envelope with pores; it controls the cell and stores the hereditary material.
Mitochondria are double-membraned, have inner cristae, carry their own DNA, and are the sites of aerobic respiration.
Ribosomes are non-membranous and are the sites of protein synthesis; rough ER carries them, smooth ER does not.
Lysosomes are enzyme-filled vesicles that digest worn-out material and are called suicide bags.
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and all membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.
A plant cell has a cellulose wall, plastids and one large permanent vacuole; an animal cell has none of these.
The cell wall is fully permeable; the cell membrane is selectively permeable and controls transport.
examFocus: Cell theory questions want three separate points with three separate names and years — one blended paragraph loses marks even when the biology is right.
'Name an organelle and state its function' expects the function in the same sentence: 'mitochondria, site of aerobic respiration', not 'mitochondria' alone.
The prokaryote versus eukaryote table is the highest-yield answer in this chapter; learn it as a table, not as scattered facts.
In a labelled diagram, labels must sit outside the cell and be joined by unbroken straight leader lines; do not write the function on the diagram itself.

vocabulary.meaning: All living things are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells.
A membrane-bounded structure within a cell with a specialised role.
A cell without a true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
A cell with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Region holding the free circular DNA of a prokaryote.
A plant-only organelle such as the chloroplast, chromoplast or leucoplast.
The outward pressure of a swollen vacuole pressing the membrane against the cell wall.
A vesicle of digestive enzymes that breaks down worn-out cell parts.

questions.prompt: Which scientist completed cell theory by proposing that all cells arise from pre-existing cells?
questions.explanation: Virchow added the third part of cell theory in 1855 with the phrase omnis cellula e cellula, meaning every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. Schleiden had covered plants in 1838 and Schwann had extended the theory to animals in 1839.
questions.commonMistake: Remembering that Hooke named the cell (1665) and taking him for a founder of cell theory — he observed dead cork and never proposed that cells arise from other cells.

questions.prompt: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into finger-like projections called __________, which increase the surface area available for aerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Cristae are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their extensive folding packs a large membrane area into a small volume, and it is on these membranes that the enzymes of the electron transport chain sit, so more folds mean more aerobic respiration per unit volume.
questions.commonMistake: Cristae belong to the inner membrane only; the outer membrane stays smooth and surrounds the whole organelle.

questions.prompt: Which pair of structures is found in a plant cell but is never present in an animal cell?
questions.explanation: The cellulose cell wall and plastids such as chloroplasts are plant-only structures. Nuclei, mitochondria, membranes, ribosomes and Golgi apparatus occur in both cell types, while lysosomes are in fact commoner in animal cells than in plant cells.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option that contains lysosomes; lysosomes are an animal-cell feature, not a plant-cell one.

questions.prompt: Give three ways in which a prokaryotic cell differs from a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: 1. A prokaryote has no true nucleus — its DNA lies free in the nucleoid — whereas a eukaryote has a nucleus enclosed in a double nuclear envelope. 2. A prokaryote has no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or endoplasmic reticulum, while a eukaryote has them. 3. A prokaryote is smaller, about 1 to 10 micrometres, and divides by binary fission, whereas a eukaryote is about 10 to 100 micrometres and divides by mitosis.
questions.explanation: The two structural differences — absent nucleus and absent membrane organelles — are the defining ones, and the size and division difference follows from them. Any three correctly contrasted pairs earn the marks, so write each as a pair rather than as a list of prokaryote traits alone.
questions.commonMistake: Listing prokaryote features only. A difference must be stated on both sides to earn the mark.

questions.prompt: An organelle is bounded by a double membrane, has inner folds, contains its own DNA, and is the site of aerobic respiration. Which organelle is it?
questions.explanation: All four clues point to the mitochondrion: a double membrane, inner cristae, its own circular DNA, and aerobic respiration as its function. A lysosome has a single membrane and no DNA, the Golgi apparatus has a single membrane, and a ribosome is not membrane-bound at all.
questions.commonMistake: Lysosomes are also vesicular organelles, but they are single-membraned and contain enzymes rather than cristae.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion and explain how each structural feature is related to its function.
questions.answer: A mitochondrion is bounded by a double membrane: the outer membrane is smooth and encloses the organelle, while the inner membrane is deeply folded into cristae. The folding greatly increases the surface area available for the enzymes of aerobic respiration, so more energy can be released in the same volume. Inside the inner membrane is the matrix, a fluid containing enzymes, ribosomes and a small circular DNA molecule, which allows some mitochondrial proteins to be made on site. The mitochondrion is thus the site where aerobic respiration takes place and energy is released in the usable form ATP.
questions.explanation: The answer must link structure to function twice: cristae give surface area for respiration, and the matrix plus its own DNA make the organelle partly self-sufficient. Stating structure with no functional link, or function with no structure, forfeits part of the mark.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the folds 'cristae' but attributing them to the outer membrane. The cristae are always of the inner membrane.

questions.prompt: A single-celled organism is found living in pond water. Under a microscope it has a clearly membrane-bound nucleus, several mitochondria, and a contractile vacuole that regularly expels water, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. Identify the type of cell, and state two features that show it is not a prokaryote and two that show it is not a plant cell.
questions.answer: It is a eukaryotic animal-like cell, such as an amoeba. It is not a prokaryote because it has a membrane-bound nucleus containing the DNA, and because it possesses membrane-bound organelles including mitochondria. It is not a plant cell because it lacks a rigid cellulose cell wall, and because it has no plastids such as chloroplasts. The contractile vacuole for expelling excess water and the irregular shape confirmed by the absence of a wall are typical of a free-living amoeboid cell.
questions.explanation: Work through the classification in the order prokaryote or eukaryote, then plant or animal. The nucleus and membrane organelles settle the first distinction; the absent wall and absent plastids settle the second. Naming the organism correctly follows from those two steps, and each required point must be tied to a stated observation rather than asserted.
questions.commonMistake: Naming an amoeba without giving the four structural reasons — the name alone earns nothing here.

questions.prompt: Explain why lysosomes are sometimes called suicide bags of the cell.
questions.answer: A lysosome is a vesicle produced by the Golgi apparatus and filled with powerful hydrolytic enzymes. If the lysosome membrane ruptures, those enzymes are released into the cytoplasm and digest the cell's own organelles and structures, destroying the cell from within. This is why the name suicide bag is used.
questions.explanation: The explanation has two linked parts — enzymes inside, and what happens when the membrane breaks. Mentioning only that lysosomes contain enzymes does not explain the name.
questions.commonMistake: Describing lysosomes as digesting food vacuoles. That is their normal digestive role; the name comes from self-digestion after rupture.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not a function of the cell wall?
options: Prevention of bursting when the cell absorbs water
Control of what enters and leaves the cell
Support that gives the plant cell its shape
questions.answer: Control of what enters and leaves the cell
questions.explanation: Controlling passage is the job of the cell membrane, which is selectively permeable. The cell wall is fully permeable and cannot select anything that crosses it; its roles are support, protection and restraining the membrane against turgor pressure so the cell does not lyse.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing selective permeability to the wall because it sits outside the cell. Only the membrane is selective.

questions.prompt: The endoplasmic reticulum exists in two forms: the ______ form, studded with ribosomes and concerned with protein synthesis, and the ______ form, which synthesises lipids and detoxifies harmful substances.
questions.explanation: The rough endoplasmic reticulum carries ribosomes on its outer surface, which is why it appears rough, and these ribosomes build proteins that are threaded into the ER lumen for modification and transport. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and performs lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism and detoxification.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the two forms. Anchoring the word ribosomes to rough ER makes the distinction reliable.

questions.prompt: A cell is observed to contain chlorophyll, a large central sac of fluid, and a rigid outer layer of cellulose. State three structures you would expect to find in this cell that would be absent from a typical animal cell, and name the organelle in which the chlorophyll is located.
questions.answer: You would expect a cellulose cell wall, plastids — including the chloroplasts that hold the chlorophyll — and one large permanent central vacuole holding cell sap, none of which is present in an animal cell. A typical animal cell is bounded by the membrane alone, stores food as glycogen rather than starch, and has only small temporary vacuoles if any. The chlorophyll itself lies in the chloroplast, specifically within the thylakoid membranes of its internal membrane system.
questions.explanation: The three observations each map to one plant-only structure: cellulose layer to the cell wall, chlorophyll to plastids, and large fluid sac to the permanent vacuole. Naming the chloroplast completes the question, and the extra contrast with animal storage shows why the cell is classed as a plant cell.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the chlorophyll is in the cytoplasm. Chlorophyll is held in the chloroplast, which is itself inside the cell.
